extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying foundational principles that define what constitutes a patentable invention, the required disclosure/consideration, and how to determine the proper scope of a patent (including equivalents and general claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent as a grant of exclusive right in exchange for disclosure (not a monopoly)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent for a useful invention is ... the grant by the government to the author of a new and useful invention, of the exclusive right, for a term of years, of practising that invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the bargain/consideration: the public receives the invention (immediate practice under patent and the right to practise it after expiration) in exchange for granting the inventor exclusive rights. Distinguishes modern patents from old English monopolies and cites the Statute of Monopolies' exception for new manufactures (term of 21 years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure / deposit / enablement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: He is required to deposit in the archives of the government a full and exact description in writing of the whole process, so framed that others can practise the invention from the description itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to prevent concealment of the process and to ensure the invention becomes available to the public after the patent term. This is presented as the public's part of the bargain and a fundamental patent requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent subject-matter limitation to new and useful effects in matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent law relates to a great and comprehensive class of discoveries and inventions of some new and useful effect or result in matter, not referable to the department of the fine arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly excludes literary, musical, and fine-arts inventions from the patent domain; the focus is on changes in the relations of particles of matter producing new effects or results useful to mankind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention includes application of natural laws, forces, or properties of matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of such new arrangements is to produce some new effect or result, by calling into activity some latent law, or force, or property, by means of which the new effect or result may be accomplished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by examples: steam-engine (application of expansive power of steam), hot-air blast in iron manufacture (introducing caloric), and manufacturing machinery. Point: invention is more than mere new arrangement of particles; it embraces the application of natural law to produce a result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle/essence of an invention is the effect or result produced
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a characteristic, an essence, or purpose of every invention, which ... has been termed by jurists its principle; and this can ordinarily be perceived ... by observing the powers or qualities of matter ... developed and put in action by that arrangement of matter, and the effect or result produced by their application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'principle' (i.e., the effect produced by applying a law of nature or property of matter) is what is protected; form or exact arrangement are secondary unless they are themselves the essence of the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery and application of a natural law or force may be patentable as applied
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery and application of a new force or law of nature, as a means of producing an effect or result in matter never before produced, may in some cases be the subject of a patentable invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies limitation: a law of nature cannot be appropriated in the abstract, but if an inventor produces a practical effect by applying the law, he may appropriate that application (i.e., claim the application insofar as others practicing it would be piracy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation/scope test — piracy of the original invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The truth, law, property, or quality of matter, which, by reason of its application, enters into the essence of an invention, may be appropriated, to the extent of every application which, according to the principles of law and the rules of logic, is to be deemed piracy of the original invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the test for how far an inventor's appropriation reaches: any later application that effectively copies or 'pirates' the original invention's application of a law/property is within the inventor's claim. Examples throughout (hot-air blast, steam application) show application to varied apparatus still may be piracy if same effect by same agent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted breadth of general claims applying known properties or laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions which consist in the application of the known qualities of substances extend the appropriation of the inventor to those qualities in the same manner and in the same sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Walton's use of india-rubber to give elasticity to card backs — patent held to cover giving elasticity and flexibility by india-rubber however applied; evaporating sugar by forcing air through liquid — any apparatus applying the same law to same purpose may practise the same invention. But caution: appropriation is confined to the inventor's application, not the abstract law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on abstract appropriation — cannot patent a law in the abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: When it has been laid down that a 'principle' ... cannot be the subject of a patent, the doctrine, rightly understood, asserts only that a law, property, or rule cannot, in the abstract, be appropriated by any man; but if an inventor ... produces an effect practically by the application of a law, he may so far appropriate that law, as to be entitled to say that whoever applies the same law to produce the same effect ... practises or makes use of his invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes the boundary: protection covers the applied use producing the practical result, not the underlying abstract scientific principle per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents / immaterial changes — non-essential form changes do not avoid the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Where form, arrangement of matter, proportion, method of construction, or apparatus employed are not of the essence of the invention, any changes introduced in them which do not effect a change in the characteristic or purpose of the invention, are changes in immaterial circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an invention's characteristic is independent of particular form, substituting an equivalent apparatus or arrangement (so long as it does not change the principle/characteristic) is merely a different mode of practising the same invention. Illustrated by machinery where different contrivances that produce the same combined operation amount to the same invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between form-only inventions and principle-based inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: When the patent is a patent for form, or particular arrangement, or for the apparatus devised to accomplish a particular effect, changes in these respects will be changes in the subject-matter of the invention; but in cases where the invention has a characteristic or an aggregate of characteristics, independent of particular form ... changes in these things amount only to the substitution of one equivalent for another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule for claim drafting and claim construction: determine whether the invention is the particular form/arrangement (narrow claim) or the underlying characteristic/principle (permits broader claim covering equivalents). Use this to assess infringement and claim breadth.
